findings.location: sections/homily/10-homily.tex lines 43-45 ('Who is that servant? St~Augustine answers that every one of us is both men in this story at once. We owe God a debt we cannot pay. And somewhere there is someone who owes us.')
findings.problem: Unchanged since iteration 1: the file is byte-identical to the sealed bytes, and the passage and its locus were re-read for this review. The attributed sentence says that each of us is 'both men in this story', which a listener hears as both the forgiven servant and the fellow servant. The two glossing sentences describe only the forgiven servant's double position, a debtor to God who has a debtor of his own. That is the rule Sermon 83.2 states ('every man is at once God's debtor, and hath also some brother a debtor to himself', NPNF1-6 lines 34993-34995). Augustine's other clause, that every man is also 'bounden to his brother by some sin' (lines 34998-34999), is what would make him both men, and the speech does not say it. The listener therefore cannot tell which two men are meant.
findings.required_result: Make the attributed sentence say what the gloss says and what Augustine says, for example that every one of us stands where that servant stands, at once a debtor to God and the creditor of some brother. Alternatively, keep 'both men' and add Augustine's other clause, that every man is also bound to his brother by some sin, so that the listener hears both roles.

findings.location: sections/homily/10-homily.tex line 64 ('He goes ``straightway'', Chrysostom notices') against line 101 ('Explaining this passage, St~John Chrysostom says something startling')
findings.problem: Unchanged since iteration 1; the file is byte-identical to the sealed bytes. Chrysostom is first named by his bare surname, in a parenthetical clause, and is quoted twice more under that name (lines 71 and 85). The full form 'St John Chrysostom' first appears at the fourth mention, where it sounds like an introduction. The listener therefore meets an unexplained name first and a belated introduction later. Augustine and Aquinas are both introduced in full at first mention.
findings.required_result: Give the full name, 'St John Chrysostom', at line 64, and use the short form at line 101 and afterwards.

findings.location: sections/homily/10-homily.tex lines 40-41 ('And the servant asks only for time. He is given the whole debt.')
findings.problem: In current English, to be 'given' a debt means to be made to owe it. The intended sense is that the whole debt is remitted, and that needs 'forgiven'. The obsolete sense of 'give' as 'remit' is not available to a modern assembly. The sentence announces the parable's first gift in a homily whose subject is a debt that is forgiven and then 'comes back'. Its literal sense is the opposite of the intended one, at the place where the contrast with 'asks only for time' should be clearest. The witness the speech follows here says it plainly: 'He gave more than he asked, remission and forgiveness of the entire debt' (Chrysostom, Hom. 61.3, NPNF1-10 lines 34993-34995). Most listeners will recover the sense from the contrast, and the next movement opens 'the king forgives with a word', so this is advisory only. I noticed it on this cold reading. The sentence is unchanged since iteration 1, and the finding gates nothing.
findings.required_result: Say 'He is forgiven the whole debt', or 'He is given the remission of the whole debt', keeping the contrast with 'asks only for time'. No other change is needed.

summary: Cold re-review of the homily 'The Words That Saved Him' (homily.tex; sections/homily/10-homily.tex and 90-note.tex) and of the two REVIEW_SCOPE files, research/production-review.md and research/artifacts.json. I hash-checked all ten sealed files. They are byte-identical to the iteration-1 seal. Intervention 0001 and commit b9786e912, which touches scripts/_tooling.py and tool files but nothing in the leaf, confirm that the re-entry was seal-only. I read the spoken body through as a listener would hear it and re-verified it independently. A script found all 24 quoted spans (331 words) in the tracked witnesses, whose SHA-256 digests I recomputed and which match the records: the Challoner Matthew and Ephesians tables (Mt 18:26, 28, 29, 32, 34, 35; Eph 6:12; Mt 20:2 for the paraphrase); NPNF1-6 Sermon 83 (NPNF 33) sections 2, 4, 7 and 8 and Sermon 58 (NPNF 8, 'Again on the Lord's Prayer') section 8; NPNF1-10 Hom. 61 in Matth. sections 3-4; NPNF1-13 Hom. 22 in Eph., whose wrath passage lies in the moral part after vv. 10-13; and the 1861 payload, lines 173-175. I read each attribution in its context. I read Aquinas, Super Matth. c. 18 on v. 35, in the 1745 OCR (Hic videtur innuere ... Sed hoc non videtur ... Dicuntur autem redire per ingratitudinem). I read the 1861 Introit, Secret, Communion and Postcommunion English on the registered scan's page images, using a copy whose SHA-256 matched 85034c90 (PDF pp. 459 and 461). Every quotation matches its witness. Every attribution stays within what its author says, and the joins the note claims as the homily's own are not credited to a Father in the speech. The argument passes the text-substitution test. Its decisive turn is the fellow servant's plea repeating the servant's own words (Mt 18:26, 29), which Chrysostom himself observes. That turn moves the hearer from 'has he deserved pardon?' to 'do I recognize my own prayer in his mouth?'. The speech carries the remission through the Cross, the empty tomb and Baptism (Augustine 83.7), then to the Secret's one sacrifice and the Postcommunion, before the consequence for the brother. The Epistle, Introit, Offertory, Communion and Collect each serve that argument and are not merely listed. I counted 1,442 spoken words, 114 sentences, a mean of 12.6 words and a longest of 39 (a Chrysostom quotation): 11.1 to 12.0 minutes at 120 to 130 words a minute, by arithmetic only. The note's figures, loci, routes and relation are accurate, and it claims no timed delivery. The new production-review entries are accurate as checked: the PDF and aux hashes, the 3, 37 and 12 page counts, the 2,356, 24,876 and 9,384 extracted words, the 27 render inputs in artifacts.json, which all re-hash, and the upstream seals of 16, 21 and 1,813 files plus 13 chronology computation inputs, which all still match. Limits: no one has spoken or timed the text. Aquinas was read on OCR, not the facsimile. Verdict: PASS. The iteration-1 advisories HOM-006 and HOM-007 stand unchanged, and one new oral-precision advisory, HOM-008, is added.
